name: Lalbagh Botanical Garden
blurb: A 240-acre garden built around a glass house and a 3-billion-year-old rock outcrop. Best before 8am, when it belongs to walkers and mynas.
try: Walk the glass-house lawns before 8am, when it still belongs to walkers.
Climb the Lalbagh rock - it's older than the city by a few billion years.

name: Cubbon Park
blurb: The city's green lung, threading past the High Court and State Library. Car-free on Sunday mornings.
try: Run or cycle the car-free roads 5:30-8am, or on Sunday mornings.
Cut through to the High Court and State Library instead of looping the same path.

name: Indian Music Experience
blurb: India's first interactive music museum, opened in 2019 with backing from the Brigade Group - three floors and nine galleries running from classical to folk to Bollywood, plus an outdoor Sound Garden where the Humming Stone and Storm Drum turn the science of sound into something you touch.
try: Walk the nine galleries in order, classical through Bollywood, before heading outside.
Play the Sound Garden yourself - Humming Stone and Storm Drum are hands-on, not behind glass.

name: Chowdiah Memorial Hall
blurb: A working concert hall built in 1980 as a tribute to violinist T. Chowdiah, shaped like a giant seven-stringed violin at 1:100 scale, right down to a 140-foot steel bow. Still hosts real Carnatic and Hindustani concerts, not just a photo stop.
try: Catch an actual Carnatic or Hindustani concert, not just the violin-shaped exterior.
Walk the 1:100-scale bow - it's a working hall, not a sculpture park.

name: Sankey Tank
blurb: A 37-acre lake dug in 1882 as a drinking-water reservoir, now one of the city's steadiest walking and jogging spots - a paved loop (not a full circuit), an open gym, and a regular crowd of morning walkers who know each other by face.
try: Do the paved lakeside loop, then the open gym if you want a short daily circuit.
Go at dusk when the water takes the last of the light.

name: Museum of Art & Photography (MAP)
blurb: A private museum built on Abhishek Poddar's decades of collecting, opened February 2023 on Kasturba Road - five floors and 44,000 sq ft carrying Indian art, textiles, photography and design from the 12th century to now, with a rooftop cafe to end the visit.
try: Start with the permanent collection, 12th century onward, then whatever's showing on top of it.
End at the rooftop cafe - the building is meant to be climbed floor by floor, not rushed.

name: Veena Stores & Thindi Beedi
blurb: A benne masale dosa counter with no seating and no fuss, on the same lane as a dozen other breakfast stalls locals actually rotate through.
try: Stand at the counter for a benne masale dosa. There are no tables.
Grazing the rest of Thindi Beedi is the point; don't stop at one stall.

name: MTR (Mavalli Tiffin Room)
blurb: Opened as the Brahmin Coffee Club in 1924, renamed MTR in 1960 - the place that invented rava idli by accident, during a WWII rice shortage. Shut for six years after the 1975 Emergency's price caps rather than cut quality, and reopened in 1981. Still run by the same family, four generations on.
try: Order rava idli - they invented it here - and filter kaapi in a steel tumbler.
Go on a weekday morning; weekends are a different restaurant.

name: Bhaskar's Mane Holige
blurb: Started in 2015 on D.V.G Road, next to Upahara Darshini - self-described as Bangalore's first shop built entirely around holige (puran poli). Grown since into multiple own and franchise outlets across the city, plus outposts in Hubballi, Mangaluru and Mumbai.
try: Try a few varieties beyond the classic - a wide holige menu is the whole point.
D.V.G Road, next to Upahara Darshini - the original the rest of the chain grew out of.

name: Corner House
blurb: Opened in 1982 as a small fast-food joint on the corner of Residency Road - ice cream wasn't even the focus at first. That changed with Death By Chocolate, now ranked among TasteAtlas's 100 most iconic ice creams in the world. The chocolate fudge recipe is named Sheila's Fudge, after the family matriarch.
try: The Death by Chocolate is the reason the city still uses this as a landmark.
Any branch works; the Residency Road original is the story, not a better scoop.

name: Vidhana Soudha
blurb: India's largest legislative building, built 1952-56 in granite and porphyry because Kengal Hanumanthaiah wanted it to read as a temple, not a bungalow - Neo-Dravidian in style, floodlit end to end on Sundays and public holidays. Guided interior walking tours only opened to the public in June 2025.
try: Catch it floodlit on a Sunday evening or a public holiday - the whole facade lights up.
Book the guided walking tour (Sundays, 2nd/4th Saturdays) for the interior - Aadhaar and advance registration required.

name: CTR (Shri Sagar)
blurb: Opened as Central Tiffin Room in the 1920s by Y.V. Subramanyam and his brothers - sold and re-established as Shree Sagar in the 1950s, then formally renamed Shri Sagar in 1992 by a new owner. Regulars still just call it CTR: the benne masale dosa reference point everyone else in the city gets compared to.
try: Benne masale dosa at the counter, standing - a tradition here across generations, whatever the sign out front said that decade.
Don't expect seating theatre - this is a tiffin room that got famous.

name: Brahmin's Coffee Bar
blurb: Standing-only since January 1965, four items on the menu - idli, vada, kara bath, kesari bath - and a chutney so central to the place that they never bothered adding sambar.
try: Four items only: idli, vada, kara bath, kesari bath. Order all of them.
Drink the kaapi standing. That is how this counter works.

name: Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace
blurb: Started by Hyder Ali in 1781 inside Bangalore Fort's walls, finished by Tipu Sultan a decade later - an all-teakwood Indo-Islamic palace that served as the British secretariat until 1868. Now an ASI-run museum with Tipu-era weapons, jewellery, and a reproduction of his mechanical Tiger Throne.
try: The museum upstairs - Tipu-era weapons, jewellery, and a reproduction of his mechanical Tiger Throne.
The palace still sits inside what's left of Bangalore Fort's walls - walk the old fort area while you're there.

name: Airlines Hotel
blurb: Open-air since 1968, tables set under old banyan trees - one of the first drive-in eateries in the city, and still the most relaxed darshini experience going.
try: Sit under the banyan trees - the open-air tables are the point.
Come for breakfast or a slow lunch, not a quick grab.

name: Karavalli
blurb: Running since 1990, styled after a Mangalorean home under tamarind trees - chefs are sent to the coast to learn recipes directly from families, not from a cookbook. Chef Naren Thimmaiah has led the kitchen since nearly the start.
try: Ask what's come in from the coast that day; the kitchen changes with the catch.
This is a sit-down meal, not a darshini - budget the evening.

name: Freedom Park
area: Central Business District, near City Railway Station
blurb: Built on the site of Bengaluru's old Central Jail - the same walls that held Atal Bihari Vajpayee and L.K. Advani during the 1975 Emergency - and reopened as a public park in 2008. Part of the grounds is still formally set aside for protest; it hosted Anna Hazare's 2011 Lokpal fast. Freedom-fighter sculptures and a central tower anchor the rest of the space.
try: Walk past the freedom-fighter sculptures and the central tower before deciding what you think of the space.
Check if anything's being protested that week - part of the park is formally kept for it, not just tolerated.

name: Mangalore Pearl
blurb: Home-style Mangalorean seafood since 2004, started by an ex-IT professional who wanted to bring his hometown's cooking to the city - neer dosa, sannas, and a whole chalkboard of fish and prawn preparations.
try: Go for kori rotti or a fish curry if you want Mangalorean cooking without the drive.
It's home-style, not plated for photographs.

name: National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA)
blurb: Housed in Manikyavelu Mansion, a century-old Palace Road bungalow first built for merchant Haji Sir Ismail Sait - restored and opened as NGMA's southern branch in 2009. About 500 works across two floors, 18th century to now: Raja Ravi Varma, Jamini Roy, Amrita Sher-Gil and Tagore among them.
try: Two floors, 18th century to now - Raja Ravi Varma and Amrita Sher-Gil are the names to look for.
The mansion itself is worth a slow look - a century-old Palace Road bungalow, not a purpose-built gallery.

name: Searock
blurb: Coastal cooking that ranges wider than most - Mangalore, Kundapur, and Karwar styles all on one menu.
try: Try a Kundapur or Karwar dish, not only the Mangalore hits.
Share a few coastal plates rather than one heavy curry.

name: Kamat Bugle Rock
blurb: The Jolada Rotti Oota reference point - unlimited North Karnataka thali on a banana leaf, live Carnatic music playing through lunch.
try: Unlimited Jolada Rotti Oota on a banana leaf - eat with your hands.
This is the North Karnataka thali reference; don't treat it as a snack.

name: Visvesvaraya Industrial and Technological Museum
blurb: Opened in 1962 on Kasturba Road, named for engineer Sir M. Visvesvaraya - hands-on galleries running from a jet engine and Tesla coils to a 1:1 Wright Flyer replica and an animatronic Spinosaurus, plus a planetarium on the same grounds.
try: Fun Science and the Electro Technic gallery - Tesla coils and Van de Graaff generators, hands-on.
The Wright Flyer replica and the animatronic Spinosaurus are the two that stop kids in their tracks.

name: Halli Mane
blurb: Jolada rotti, ennegayi, and badanekayi palya with a village-mess feel. People drive across the city for it.
try: Jolada rotti with ennegayi and badanekayi palya - the village-mess plates.
It's a full meal; go hungry.

name: Sri Venkateshwara North Karnataka Foods
blurb: A cheap, no-frills Jolada Rotti Oota - two rotis, rice, sambar, rasam, and curd for around a hundred rupees, masala buttermilk and gulab jamun extra.
try: The cheap Jolada Rotti Oota: two rotis, rice, sambar, rasam, curd.
VV Puram after sunset if you want the street as well as the plate.

name: Rangoli Metro Art Center
blurb: Built by BMRCL on top of the MG Road metro station and opened in 2013 - three galleries (Vismaya, Chaya, Belaku), a kids' play area called Chilipili, an upper walkway called Hoovina Haadi, and an open-air performance space called Bayalu, free to walk through.
try: Walk Hoovina Haadi, the upper walkway, then drop into whichever of the three galleries has a show up.
Free and partly open-air - an easy stop before or after an MG Road evening.

name: Sendhoor Coffee House
blurb: A neighbourhood filter coffee spot doing the same soft idli-crisp vada-strong kaapi routine, minus the queues of its more famous neighbours.
try: Idli, vada, and a strong filter kaapi. That is the visit.
Neighbourhood pace; don't expect a menu tour.

name: Araku Coffee
blurb: A two-storeyed flagship with an in-house roastery and a bookstore built in - beans grown on the Araku Valley's own estates, further proof Bengaluru's specialty coffee scene runs deep.
try: A pour-over or filter from the in-house roast, then browse the bookstore upstairs.
This is a sit-and-stay cafe, not a stand-and-go kaapi.

name: Bannerghatta National Park
blurb: Established 1970, declared a national park in 1974 - 260 sq km of scrub and deciduous forest home to elephants, tigers, leopards and sloth bears, and part of a corridor linking the BR Hills and Sathyamangalam forests. The attached Biological Park (2002) runs the 6km safari loop most visitors actually come for.
try: The safari loop in the Biological Park - elephants, tigers and leopards from inside the bus.
Go early; it's a real forest corridor to BR Hills, not a zoo enclosure loop.

name: Third Wave Coffee Roasters
blurb: Founded 2016 by three childhood friends chasing specialty coffee in an industry still in its infancy in India - the flagship that helped start Bengaluru's third-wave scene, roasting beans sourced from Chikmagalur.
try: A single-origin pour-over if you want specialty, not filter-kaapi nostalgia.
Laptop-friendly; pick a quieter outlet if you're working.

name: Attara Kacheri (Karnataka High Court)
area: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Road, opposite Vidhana Soudha
blurb: Built 1864-68 by Richard Hieram Sankey as the Public Offices Building - Neoclassical, gneiss and brick under red-ochre plaster, twelve Ionic columns a side. The name comes from Chikka Devaraja Wadiyar's 18-department (attara-kacheri) Mughal-style administration, adopted in 1699. Became the Karnataka High Court's seat once the legislature and secretariat moved to Vidhana Soudha in 1956.
try: Look at it beside Vidhana Soudha across the road - same street, two very different colonial-to-independence stories.
It's a working High Court, not a museum - view from outside, don't expect to walk in.

name: Dyu Art Cafe
blurb: Part gallery, part cafe, part quiet workspace - paintings on every wall, two floors of greenery, and enough breakfast-to-dessert range to justify hours here.
try: Work or read downstairs; the paintings are the décor, not a gallery hop.
Stay for a slow coffee rather than a photo of the façade.

name: Sri Venkateshwara Sweetmeat Stall
blurb: Started by Venkatachala Shetty in 1954 and still widely called the best Mysore Pak in India - ghee-heavy, soft, and made the same way seventy years on.
try: Mysore Pak from the stall that's been arguing it's the best since 1954.
Buy a box to take; this is not a sit-down sweet shop.

name: Halasuru Someshwara Temple
blurb: Chola-era origins from around the 12th-13th century, expanded through the Hoysala and Vijayanagara periods, with major additions under Kempe Gowda II - one of the city's oldest surviving temples, in the Vijayanagara style. Its own founding story splits in two: one account has Kempegowda I dreaming of Someshwara after a hunting trip, another credits a different local chieftain, Jayappa Gowda.
try: The pillared mantapa carvings - Vijayanagara-era work, older than most of what's left in the city centre.
Pair it with Ulsoor Lake, a short walk away, for one Halasuru morning.

name: Asha Sweet Center
blurb: A Bengaluru mithai institution since 1951 - Mysore Pak, kaju katli, rasmalai, and a bakery counter alongside, trusted for festive gifting for three generations.
try: Mysore Pak or kaju katli, plus whatever the bakery counter has that day.
Any outlet; it's an institution, not a single-room pilgrimage.

name: Atta Galatta
blurb: A bookstore built around Indian and regional-language writing, with a steady calendar of readings and open mics - one of the city's real literary hubs, not just a shop. Moved here from Koramangala in 2022.
try: Browse Indian and regional-language shelves; check what's on the events calendar.
It's a bookshop that wants you to linger, not a cafe with books.

name: Sri Panchalinga Nageshwara Temple
blurb: Five Shiva lingas in one complex - Nageshwara and Nagareshwara, the oldest, were built by Ganga-dynasty rulers in the 9th-10th centuries. An inscription here from around 890 CE records a battle at 'Bengaluru' - the earliest known appearance of the city's name, centuries before Kempe Gowda.
try: Find the 890 CE inscription - the oldest known written record of the name 'Bengaluru.'
Five lingas in one complex; take the time to see all five, not just the main shrine.

name: Blossom Book House
blurb: New and secondhand books since 2002, several floors deep, with a reputation for rare and out-of-print finds that keeps collectors coming back.
try: Go upstairs for secondhand and odd finds; Church Street is the hunt.
Budget time - several floors deep since 1962.

name: Sri Gavi Gangadhareshwara Swamy Temple
blurb: A cave temple carved from a single natural rock, renovated by Kempe Gowda I in the 16th century after his release from a five-year imprisonment. Its real trick is astronomical: on Makar Sankranti and a few other dates, sunlight threads between the horns of the Nandi outside and lands directly on the linga inside the cave.
try: Time a visit for Makar Sankranti if you can - the sunlight-through-Nandi's-horns alignment is the whole point.
Look at the monolithic stone discs in the forecourt; nobody's fully explained what they were for.

name: Pecos
blurb: A retro rock pub that has barely changed - cheap drinks, classic rock on the speakers, and a regular crowd that has been coming back for decades.
try: Cheap drinks, classic rock, no redesign - that's the night.
Go with people who like pubs that haven't been restyled.

name: Ulsoor Lake
blurb: One of the city's oldest lakes, dating to Kempegowda and later expanded under the British - a jogging path along the water, boating, and an island in the middle, minutes from MG Road.
try: Walk the bund in the morning; it's one of Kempegowda's old tanks, enlarged later.
Don't come for boating theatre - it's a city lake, used as a lake.

name: Sri Dakshinamukha Nandi Tirtha Kalyaani Kshetra
blurb: A 400-year-old shrine that vanished under sand and silt as Malleswaram grew around it, with no gopuram tower to mark it from the road - only excavated back into view in 1997. Its south-facing stone Nandi has water flowing continuously from its mouth; where the water comes from is still unexplained.
kn: ಶ್ರೀ ದಕ್ಷಿಣಮುಖ ನಂದಿ ತೀರ್ಥ ಕಲ್ಯಾಣಿ ಕ್ಷೇತ್ರ
try: Find it below street level, opposite the Gangamma temple - there's no tower to spot it by.
Watch the water flow from the Nandi's mouth; nobody knows the source.

name: Agara Lake
blurb: A 98-acre lake with a full perimeter jogging track, popular with the HSR and Koramangala crowd for a reason - clean, well kept, and rarely too crowded to actually run.
try: The full perimeter jog, popular with HSR and Koramangala for a reason.
Early or late; midday is just a hot loop.

name: Puttenahalli Lake
blurb: A small lake restored and maintained by the neighbourhood around it rather than the city. Quiet, good for birdwatching, a genuine community effort.
try: A short walk maintained by the neighbourhood, not a destination park.
Treat it as a local pause if you're already in JP Nagar.

name: Dodda Basavana Gudi (Bull Temple)
blurb: Built by Kempe Gowda I in 1537 - the world's largest Nandi monolith, 4.5m tall and 6.5m long, carved from a single block of granite. The neighbourhood takes its name directly from this temple: basava is bull, gudi is temple. Still the anchor of Kadlekai Parishe every November-December, when farmers pile the season's first groundnut harvest around it.
try: Stand close enough to take in the scale - one block of granite, 4.5m tall.
Come back for Kadlekai Parishe if you're here between November and December.

name: Gandhi Bazaar
blurb: A flower-and-condiment market that has run since well before independence - puja items, fresh produce, and the DVG Road stretch that anchors old Basavanagudi.
try: Buy flowers, coconut, and puja items the way the market has always sold them.
Combine with a Gandhi Bazaar breakfast; the street is the visit.

name: KR Market (City Market)
blurb: The city's biggest wholesale market - flowers, fruit, vegetables, and spices sold by the sackload since long before Bengaluru had supermarkets. Go early, before 8am, for it at its most alive.
try: Go at dawn for flowers by the sack, not a boutique browse.
It's wholesale chaos - wear shoes you don't mind.

name: Kote Sri Prasanna Venkataramana Swamy Temple
blurb: Built in 1689 by Chikka Devaraja Wadiyar in Dravidian-Vijayanagara style, next to what was once the Wodeyar residence and later Tipu Sultan's palace - kote means fort in Kannada, and this is the temple inside the old one. Vaikuntha Ekadashi here draws crowds every year.
kn: ಕೋಟೆ ಶ್ರೀ ಪ್ರಸನ್ನ ವೆಂಕಟರಮಣ ಸ್ವಾಮಿ ದೇವಸ್ಥಾನ
say: Kote Sri Prasanna Venkataramana Swamy Devasthana
try: Pair it with Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace next door - same old fort, two very different buildings.
Time it for Vaikuntha Ekadashi if you want the temple at full crowd.

name: Karnataka Chitrakala Parishath
blurb: An 18-gallery art complex founded in 1960, with a permanent collection of Mysore paintings and leather puppetry - and Chitra Santhe, the city's open-air art fair, held here every January.
try: The Mysore painting rooms in the permanent collection, then whichever show is up.
Eighteen galleries: pick two, don't march the lot.

name: Shree Banashankari Devi Temple
blurb: Founded in 1915 when a devotee (sources give his name as either Subramanya Shetty or Somanna Shetty) brought the deity from the original 7th-century Banashankari Amma temple near Badami and installed her here. The south Bengaluru neighbourhood took its name from the temple, not the other way around.
try: Note the Badami connection - the deity here was carried from the 7th-century original near Badami in 1915.
The Banashankari neighbourhood and metro station both take their name from this temple, not the reverse.

name: Srinivasa Brahmins Bakery
blurb: An Iyengar bakery running since 1956, part of the wave of bakeries Iyengar Brahmin migrants from Hassan set up across the city. Famous for Congress kadlekai - spiced split peanuts, named after the 1969 party split - stuffed into a butter-laced khara bun.
try: Iyengar bakery classics: toast, khara bun, and whatever just came out.
It's a counter, not a cafe.

name: Thom's Bakery
blurb: The city's reference point for the cream bun - an Iyengar-bakery classic, essentially a filled doughnut topped with coconut flakes and tutti-frutti, not a Western cream bun at all.
try: The cream bun is the city's reference version - that's the order.
Take away; this is a bakery queue.

name: CSI St. Mark's Cathedral
area: West end of MG Road, MacIver Town
blurb: Foundation laid 1808, completed 1812, consecrated 1816 - English Baroque, modelled on St Paul's Cathedral in London, with a dome and semi-circular chancel. Church of South India (Anglican tradition) today, one of the oldest churches still standing in the city.
try: Look up at the dome and chancel - a deliberate small echo of St Paul's in London.
One of the oldest churches standing in the city; check service and visiting hours before you go.

name: VB Bakery
blurb: The bakery anchoring the start of Thindi Beedi - the Congress Khara Bun here, butter and spiced peanuts packed into a soft bun, is the one regulars name first.
try: Congress Khara Bun at the start of Thindi Beedi, then walk the lane.
Butter and spice; don't overthink the rest of the tray.

name: Koshy's Automatic Bakery
blurb: Baking since 1940 - egg puffs and glazed doughnuts are the reason people cross the city for this one, plum cake included every December.
try: Egg puffs and glazed doughnuts - people cross the city for those two.
Any outlet; the 1940 story is the brand, not a single room.

name: St. Mary's Basilica
blurb: Started as a thatched chapel in 1803, rebuilt in the current Gothic form between 1856 and 1882, and raised to Basilica status by Pope Paul VI in 1973. The September feast draws crowds estimated at half a million over ten days, ending in a chariot procession.
try: Time it for the September feast if you want the chariot procession and the crowd it draws.
The Gothic structure took 26 years to build (1856-1882) - worth a slow look at the facade.

name: Karnataka Bhel House
blurb: A small family counter on Uma Theatre Road doing exactly one thing well - Bengaluru-style masala puri, wetter and more ragda-like than the chaat found elsewhere in India, alongside sev puri and dahi puri.
try: One thing: Bengaluru-style bhel. That's the visit.
Uma Theatre Road, standing, then move on.

name: St Patrick's Church
blurb: Foundation laid 1841, completed 1844, Gothic in style - built for the Irish soldiers garrisoned nearby, and named after their patron saint even though it was formally dedicated to the Assumption. Still standing on Brigade Road after renovations in 2000 and 2012.
try: Note the mismatch - dedicated to the Assumption, but the Irish garrison's name for it is the one that stuck.
Brigade Road right outside; easy to fold into an evening on the strip.

name: Mahalakshmi Tiffin Room (MLTR)
blurb: Been serving the same Gandhi Bazaar lane since 1926, one door down from its far more photographed neighbour. Order the khali dose - a bare, buttery dosa found almost nowhere else.
try: Khali dose - the bare, buttery dosa almost nobody else still does.
Same Gandhi Bazaar lane as the famous neighbour, without the queue theatre.

name: Atithyaa
blurb: An unlimited Karnataka thali on a kansa plate, serving the same Gandhi Bazaar crowd since 1986 - bisi bele bath, gojju, and palya that change with the season, not the menu.
try: Unlimited Karnataka thali on a kansa plate - bisi bele bath, gojju, seasonal palya.
Lunch crowd since 1986; this is a meal, not a tasting.

name: St. Francis Xavier's Cathedral
blurb: The first church here went up in 1851 under French Paris Foreign Missions Society priests; the current building was inaugurated in 1932. Became the cathedral seat when the Bangalore diocese split off from Mysore in 1940 - its twin facade domes were added for the platinum jubilee in 2009.
try: Look for the two domes on the facade - a 2009 addition, not part of the 1932 original.
It's the Bangalore diocese's cathedral, not just a parish church, since 1940.

name: Mudde Madappa Mess
blurb: A no-frills mess built entirely around ragi mudde - hot millet dumplings with saaru, rice and buttermilk, coupon at the counter, hands washed at the table.
try: Ragi mudde with saaru, rice and buttermilk - coupon at the counter, hands at the table.
Don't come for dosa. Come for millet.

name: Halli Jonne Biriyani
blurb: The donne biryani style done properly - their own 'Jonne rice' blend (seeraga samba, slow-cooked), a green masala base, and the biryani served hot in an areca-leaf donne, not a foil box.
try: Donne biryani in an areca-leaf cup: their seeraga samba 'Jonne rice,' green masala.
Eat it hot in the donne, not packed for later.

name: CSI Holy Trinity Church
area: Trinity Circle, east end of MG Road
blurb: Built by the East India Company from 1848, consecrated in 1852 - English Renaissance style, seats 700, and billed as the largest military church in south India. The stained glass and the baptismal font came from London, and even the bell was cast there, at the Mears Foundry, in 1847.
try: Find the stained-glass baptism window - shipped in from London along with the font.
Trinity Circle is the giveaway - the church gave the junction its name, not the other way round.

name: VV Puram Food Street
blurb: A single lane that turns into an open kitchen after sunset - grilled corn, kebabs, and desserts nobody outside Karnataka has heard of.
try: After sunset: grilled corn, kebabs, and sweets that don't travel outside Karnataka.
Walk the whole lane; one stall is a snack, the street is dinner.

name: C.S.I. St. John's Church
blurb: Ground broken in 1853 by Rev. R. Posnett, an assistant chaplain at St. Mark's who wanted a parish nearer the old 'Mootoocherry' area - completed by 1857, giving St. John's Hill its name. The fourth-oldest Protestant church in the city, with a distinctive red facade and steeple.
try: The red facade and steeple are the landmark - hard to miss once you know the hill.
Fourth-oldest Protestant church in the city. Go in expecting quiet.

name: Toit Brewpub
blurb: One of the city's first craft breweries, opened in 2010 as the microbrewery boom was just getting started here.
try: A house beer and a long table - this is the brewpub that normalised craft here.
Indiranagar evening, not a nightclub.

name: Amrut Distillery
blurb: The distillery behind India's first internationally launched single malt, which debuted in Glasgow in 2004 - Bengaluru's heat actually speeds up the ageing. Amrut Fusion, the label's best-known expression, followed in 2009. Tours exist but are inconsistent; call ahead rather than showing up.
try: The tour if you care how Fusion gets made; otherwise drink it in the city, not the industrial estate.
It's a distillery on Mysore Road - plan the trip, don't stumble in.

name: Jumma Masjid (Sangeen Jamia)
blurb: Bangalore's oldest mosque, built in 1790 by Haji Qazi Abdul Quddus Saheb with construction material brought specially from Srirangapatna under Tipu Sultan's patronage. Damaged by cannon fire during the Mysore wars and rebuilt in 1836 - still standing on the road that carries its name.
try: Note the Tipu Sultan connection - the stone came from Srirangapatna on his orders.
The road it's on is named after it, not the reverse - a sign of how long it's anchored the area.

name: Commercial Street
blurb: The city's fashion and export-surplus strip - clothing stores, footwear, and export-reject bargains packed into a few pedestrian-heavy lanes.
try: Walk it for clothes, shoes and export surplus, not a boutique browse.
Pair it with Chickpet a few km away for the two-mood contrast.

name: Chickpet
blurb: The old city's wholesale lanes - silk, bangles, and spice sold by weight, with a density Commercial Street doesn't try to match.
try: Go for fabric, bangles and spice by weight - old-city density, not a mall aisle.
Pair it with Commercial Street a few km away for the two-mood contrast.

name: Lakeview Milk Bar
blurb: Started in 1930 by an Englishman, James Meadow Charles, opposite Ulsoor Lake - where 1 MG Mall now stands - selling three flavours of ice cream from carts cycled around the city. Sold to a 19-year-old, Vrajlal Jamnadas, when Charles left for England in 1947; moved to its current MG Road spot in the 1970s.
try: Order off the original three flavours - vanilla, chocolate, raspberry - before the newer menu.
Remember the name's origin: Ulsoor Lake used to be visible from the first branch, long before the MG Road move.

name: Malleswaram Market
blurb: Flowers, filter coffee powder, and produce sold the way it has been for generations, a few streets from CTR.
try: Flowers, filter-coffee powder, and produce the way the neighbourhood still shops.
Pair it with Veena Stores or CTR on the same visit.

name: UB City
blurb: The city's luxury quarter - useful for seeing how Bengaluru's design and jewellery houses reinterpret Karnataka craft for a global shelf.

skipCrowd.why: A luxury mall with imported marble - striking, but tells you nothing about Karnataka craft.
skipCrowd.insteadNote: The real handloom and sandalwood work, at fixed state-run prices.

try: Look at how Bengaluru jewellery and design houses present themselves - then leave for actual craft.
Open Skip the crowd on the card if this was the royal-India photo stop.

name: Koshy's
blurb: P.O. Koshy opened a bakery here in 1940; the restaurant went up next to it in 1952 and became the city's best-known intellectual and political hangout - writers, artists and more than a few chief ministers have held court in its booths. Third-generation Koshys, Prem and Santosh, still run it. Same family as Koshy's Automatic Bakery, but a different venue.
try: Sit in for a slow breakfast or coffee - the booths, not a takeaway counter, are the point here.
Notice who's at the next table before assuming it's just a cafe; this is where the city's political and literary crowd still meets.

name: ISKCON Temple Bangalore
blurb: A modern temple complex built into a hillside, worth visiting at evening aarti even if you're not devotional.

skipCrowd.why: Long security queues and a shuffle-through pace that leaves little room to sit with it.
skipCrowd.insteadNote: A 16th-century monolithic Ganesha, tucked below Bull Temple hill, usually quieter than the climb above.

try: Evening aarti if you want the hill complex at full volume.
Open Skip the crowd for Dodda Ganapathi if you want a quieter temple.

name: Shivaji Military Hotel
blurb: Opened in 1935 in Nagarthapet by a Maharashtrian, S Mannaji Rao - a 'military hotel' in the old South Indian sense: a non-vegetarian eatery named for the military crowd that first filled these places, not an army-run mess. Moved to Jayanagar as it grew popular; donne biryani is the dish it's known for now.
try: Order the donne biryani - the dish that carried this place's reputation from Nagarthapet to Jayanagar.
Know the term going in: 'military hotel' means non-veg eatery here, not an army mess.

name: Bangalore Palace
blurb: A Tudor-style palace that has nothing to do with Rajasthani forts - a reminder that royal Karnataka architecture looked very different.

skipCrowd.why: A Tudor-Gothic building with a paid walk-through and little Karnataka history behind it.
skipCrowd.insteadNote: Mysuru Palace, ~3 hrs south - the Wodeyar seat, lit gold every Sunday evening.

try: A Tudor walk-through - useful as a reminder this isn't Rajasthan.
Open Skip the crowd if you actually wanted a royal seat: that's Mysuru.

name: Ranga Shankara
blurb: The city's best-loved theatre, running Kannada, English, and regional-language plays most nights of the week.
try: Check the week's Kannada, English, and regional plays and book a night.
It's a theatre. Stay for the play, not the lobby.

name: New Modern Hotel
blurb: Running since 1959, known less for its idli than for the bucket of sambar left on the table so you serve yourself as much as you want. Regulars have been bringing their children and grandchildren back for the same plate for decades; local lore even credits breakfast-table talk here with shaping two Kannada New Wave films, Samskara and Chomana Dudi.
try: Order one idli and let the bucket of sambar do the rest - that's the actual move here, not a full thali.
Go for a slow morning, not a quick bite; this is a sit-and-talk institution, not a grab-and-go darshini.

name: Cauvery Arts & Crafts Emporium
blurb: The state-run showroom for Karnataka craft under one roof: Mysore silk, sandalwood carving, and handloom from as far as Ilkal and Hubballi-Dharwad.
try: Mysore silk, sandalwood, and Channapatna under one state-run roof, fixed prices.
This is the craft shop; UB City is the mall.

name: Dodda Ganapathi Temple
blurb: A 16th-century monolithic Ganesha below Bull Temple hill - quieter than the city's headline temples, and a better place to actually sit.
try: Sit with the 16th-century monolithic Ganesha below Bull Temple hill.
Give it time. Don't stack it with a temple-hopping checklist.

name: The Pump House
blurb: Opened December 2018, co-founded by Chef Vishal Atreya and designed by Jatin Hukkeri of WDA - a craft brewpub built on the bet that JP Nagar shouldn't have to travel to Indiranagar or Koramangala for a decent microbrewery. Picked up Best Regional Debutant Restro-Bar (South) at the 2019 Indian Restaurant Congress Awards; a second outlet has since opened in Whitefield.
try: Try the house craft beers rather than defaulting to a familiar bottle.
JP Nagar, not Indiranagar - the founders built it precisely so you wouldn't have to make that drive.

name: Vidyarthi Bhavan
blurb: The masala dosa that went viral and stayed that way. Know the name, and know when to skip the queue.

skipCrowd.why: An hour-long wait for a table on weekends is the usual story now.
skipCrowd.insteadNote: The same benne masale dosa culture, no influencer queue, and a whole lane of breakfast stalls to graze.

try: Masala dosa if you accept the wait; otherwise open Skip the crowd.
It's famous. That is why the queue exists, and why the name still matters.

name: Turahalli Forest
blurb: 590 acres of dry deciduous forest and granite outcrops on the city's southern edge, with leopards, spotted deer and 60-plus recorded bird species - often called Bengaluru's last real forest. The reserve forest section is now off-limits to the public to protect it from the trekking, cycling and littering that used to happen there; a separate Tree Park section stays open.
try: Stick to the Tree Park section - the reserve forest itself is closed to visitors now, for the forest's sake.
Don't expect the cycling and bouldering trails from a few years ago; access has tightened since.

name: Brigade Road / MG Road
blurb: The nightlife strip of mall-brand shopping and chain restaurants you could swap for any Indian metro.

skipCrowd.why: The same strip you'd find in most Indian metros.
skipCrowd.insteadNote: Independent kitchens and bars on Indiranagar's 12th Main, run by Bengaluru people, not franchise counters.

try: Walk it once so you know the strip, then leave.
Open Skip the crowd for Indiranagar if you wanted a night out.

name: Chinita
blurb: Mexican food with proper horchata, churros, and a mole that is not watered down for an Indian palate. Go for the tacos, stay for the horchata.
try: Tacos and horchata; the mole if you want something that isn't mild-for-India.
Indiranagar or Koramangala - same kitchen idea.

name: Mini Forest, HBR Layout
blurb: A small Miyawaki-method plantation packed into a residential HBR Layout plot - dense, fast-growing native species doing in a few years what a conventional plantation takes decades to approximate. One of several such pocket forests that have gone up across the city.
try: Walk the dense planting up close - the whole point of the Miyawaki method is packing native species tight, not spacing them out.
Compare it mentally to a regular park; this is doing a different job, not competing on lawn space.

name: Chianti
blurb: An Italian spot that's been consistently good for years: pasta, lasagna, tiramisu. A safe room when you don't want to gamble.
try: Pasta or lasagna when you don't want to gamble on a new place.
Tiramisu if you're already there; this is a consistent, not a trendy, room.

name: RnR Biriyani
blurb: Donne-style biryani on a grandmother's recipe they still sell as "Taste of 1953" - short-grain, green masala, Bengaluru's own, not the Hyderabadi kind. The kitchen behind it is SRR Foods; the original counter is near the Koramangala BDA complex.
try: Donne mutton or chicken biryani - the recipe is the point, not a new mash-up.
Koramangala 4th B Block, near the BDA complex; other outlets exist, same donne style.

name: Doresanipalya Forest
area: Off Bannerghatta Road, near Puttenahalli Lake
blurb: Once part of Bannerghatta National Park before the city grew around it - now an island of forest wedged between Bannerghatta Road and Puttenahalli Lake, run as a research station for forest departments studying environmental policy and tiger conservation. Every tree is labelled, and it's known for butterfly species uncommon elsewhere in the city, including the Baronet and Large Oakblue.
try: Look for the Baronet and Large Oakblue butterflies - both uncommon elsewhere in Bengaluru.
Read the tree labels as you walk; the labelling is deliberate, meant for exactly this kind of slow visit.

name: Meghana Foods
blurb: Andhra-style biryani that people actually queue for. Spicier than most. The boneless chicken biryani is the usual order.
try: Boneless chicken biryani, spicier than most of the city's Andhra counters.
Expect a queue; that's the cult, not a secret.

name: Namma SLN (Muddanna)
blurb: The Cubbonpet Muddanna line, this counter on Gandhi Bazaar Main Road - vegetarian, standing-room more often than not, built around a ghee-heavy veg palav that people in this city will argue is better than most biryani. Banana leaf, paper plate, and a sabbakki dosa if you come early enough that breakfast is still on.
try: The muddanna palav, hot, on a banana leaf - that is the dish.
Gandhi Bazaar Main Road - come early if you want the dosa side of the menu, not just the palav.

name: Umesh Dosa Point
blurb: A standing-room dosa counter on Nehru Nagar Main Road, known for ghee, pudi masala, and a bath dosa stuffed with rice bath. Not a heritage tiffin room - a neighbourhood point that people keep going back to because the dosa is actually good.
try: Pudi masala dosa or the bath dosa - those are the two that built the queue.
Stand and eat; parking and seating are not the point of this stretch of road.

name: Desi
blurb: The Bengaluru shops for Charaka, the women's handloom cooperative in Honnesara, Shivamogga district. Naturally dyed cotton, sold here since Desi Trust opened in 1997 to give that cloth a city market. Other rooms in Malleswaram, Banashankari (Seetha Circle), and Vijayanagar. This pin is the South End one.
try: Naturally dyed Charaka cotton. Ask which pieces came from Honnesara.
Other Desi rooms: Malleswaram, Seetha Circle, Vijayanagar.

name: Varnam Craft Collective
blurb: A Bengaluru social enterprise that put Channapatna lac-turnery on a city shelf: toys, jewellery, and household pieces by named artisans, including turners from the toy town. Founded by Karthik Vaidyanathan. There is a second room in Jayanagar 5th Block.
try: Channapatna pieces first, then the Kolar ceramics and other crafts they stock.
Jayanagar 5th Block if Indiranagar is the wrong side of town.
